content: The issue of iron overload at both individual and population levels necessitates the identification of a reliable indicator to assess the associated risks. Clinically, the variability in recommended and utilized ferritin thresholds creates confusion for both clinicians and patients. From a public health perspective, these differences hinder the comparison of survey data, delay the development of global estimates for iron deficiency prevalence, and obscure evaluations of the effectiveness and safety of nutritional interventions. Modern guideline development processes require a systematic and rigorous review of the literature, including an assessment of the certainty of evidence. Consequently, the evidence supporting current ferritin thresholds must be systematically reviewed to inform recommendations for the use and interpretation of ferritin levels in clinical and public health contexts. A transparent and rigorous approach should also facilitate international harmonization of ferritin thresholds or, at the very least, enable institutions to select appropriate thresholds based on the best available evidence. This approach could serve as a model for developing evidence-based thresholds for other health and development biomarkers. The World Health Organization (WHO) established a steering group in 2009, led by the Department of Nutrition and Food Safety, with representatives from various departments, including Global Capacities, Alert and Response; Essential Medicines and Health Products; Knowledge, Ethics, and Research; Health Statistics and Information Systems; and Maternal and Perinatal Health. This group oversaw the guideline development process, including evidence retrieval, assessment, and synthesis. They drafted the scope of the guideline, identified systematic review teams and guideline methodologists, finalized the planning proposal, and selected the guideline development group and external resource persons. They also managed conflicts of interest in consultation with the Office of Compliance, Risk Management, and Ethics. The steering group drafted the recommendations based on the decisions of the guideline development group, managed the peer-review process, and oversaw the dissemination of the guideline. Regional advisers from WHO regions participated in the guideline development group meetings. The guideline development group for ferritin was composed of 12 experts with diverse technical skills, perspectives, geographic representation, and gender balance. These experts included content specialists, methodologists, and representatives of potential stakeholders and beneficiaries. The group advised WHO on the scope of the guidelines, priority questions for systematic evidence reviews, the selection of critical outcomes for decision-making, and the formulation of final recommendations. The group’s initial meeting in 2010 in Panama City established the general scope, key questions, and target audience for the guideline. Four background papers were commissioned, including one on the rationale for selecting and standardizing indicators of iron status. A second meeting in 2016 in Geneva reviewed the evidence and appraised its certainty using GRADE evidence profiles. The group used the DECIDE framework to guide the formulation of recommendations, considering intervention effects, values, resources, equity, acceptability, and feasibility. External resource persons, identified by the steering group, provided insights on iron metabolism, micronutrient deficiencies, program evaluation, and systematic review development. They participated in technical presentations and discussions but did not contribute to the final decision-making on recommendation wording, direction, or strength. Systematic review teams synthesized evidence for each key question to inform the recommendations. The findings were presented at the guideline development group meeting in 2016. The systematic reviews followed Cochrane Handbook procedures and assessed the risk of bias for each study, contributing to the overall certainty of the evidence. The steering group managed potential conflicts of interest in compliance with WHO guidelines. All guideline development group members completed declarations of interest and confidentiality forms, and their curricula vitae were reviewed. Publicly available information was also assessed to identify any potential intellectual biases. All concerns were addressed in consultation with the WHO Office of Compliance, Risk Management, and Ethics. No perceived or real conflicts of interest were identified among the group members. The guideline development group identified priority questions and outcomes for the recommendations. These questions were drafted by WHO technical staff and reviewed by the steering group. A meeting in 2010 finalized the scope of the questions and ranked the outcomes and populations of interest. Serum ferritin and transferrin receptor were prioritized for thorough review. The group scored the importance of each outcome on a scale of 1 to 9, with higher scores indicating critical importance for decision-making. The final key questions and critical outcomes are listed in the guideline annex. WHO developed a project to retrieve, summarize, and assess evidence for recommendations on the use and interpretation of serum/plasma ferritin concentrations for assessing iron status in populations. Five protocols were initially developed to address specific topics through systematic reviews and raw data analysis. Systematic reviews summarized and appraised evidence based on PICO questions, following Cochrane Handbook procedures. Each study was assessed for risk of bias, contributing to the overall certainty of the evidence. The findings were synthesized with pooled estimates of effect when possible. Evidence profiles were prepared using the GRADE approach, rating the certainty of evidence as high, moderate, low, or very low based on criteria such as risk of bias, inconsistency, imprecision, indirectness, and publication bias. The guideline development group considered the certainty of evidence, the balance of benefits and harms, values and preferences, acceptability, resource implications, equity, and feasibility when formulating recommendations. Recommendations were classified as “strong” or “conditional” based on the group’s confidence in the balance of desirable and undesirable consequences. Decision-making procedures were established at the beginning of the meetings, and recommendations were approved by a two-thirds vote if unanimous consensus was not reached. The guideline was drafted by the responsible technical officer with input from the steering group and underwent technical editing and proofreading. The guideline will be disseminated through electronic media, social media, and WHO networks, with attention to improving access for stakeholders facing barriers to information. Plans for updating the guideline include monitoring research developments on iron deficiency biomarkers and conducting a formal review near the 10-year mark.
